questions.text: Explain how you would optimize rendering of a large list (10,000+ rows) in a React application.
questions.reference_answer: Use windowing / virtualization (react-window or react-virtualized) so only visible rows are mounted. Provide stable, unique key props. Memoize row components with React.memo. Avoid inline objects/functions in props to prevent re-renders. Debounce scroll handlers. If data comes from an API, paginate or use infinite scroll.

questions.text: What is the Virtual DOM and how does React use it to update the UI efficiently?
questions.reference_answer: The Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of the real DOM. On state/props change, React builds a new VDOM tree, diffs it against the previous one (reconciliation), and computes a minimal set of real-DOM mutations to apply. This batching+diffing is faster than direct DOM manipulation for most UI updates.

questions.text: When would you choose Redux over the Context API for state management in a React app, and why?
questions.reference_answer: Context API is ideal for low-frequency global values (theme, auth user, locale). Redux (or Redux Toolkit) fits when state is large, updates frequently, many distant components need the same slices, or you need middleware, devtools time-travel, caching and predictable action-based debugging. Frequent context value changes re-render every consumer, so Redux selectors keep re-renders surgical.

questions.text: How would you store and use a JWT in a React SPA securely, and what are the XSS trade-offs?
questions.reference_answer: Prefer storing the JWT in memory (or httpOnly cookie set by the server) rather than localStorage, which is readable by any injected script. Attach the token via an Axios/fetch interceptor. Use short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens, and sanitise/escape all rendered content to reduce XSS risk. Understand that httpOnly cookies bring CSRF considerations instead.

questions.text: Explain the CSS box model and how you approach building a responsive layout.
questions.reference_answer: Every element is content + padding + border + margin; box-sizing: border-box makes width calculations predictable. For responsiveness: mobile-first media queries, Flexbox for 1-D layouts, CSS Grid for 2-D layouts, relative units (%, rem, fr) and fluid images. Prefer layout with flex/grid over floats, and test across breakpoints.

questions.text: What are the Rules of Hooks in React and why do they exist? Give an example of a useful custom hook.
questions.reference_answer: Hooks must be called at the top level of a component or custom hook, never inside conditions, loops or nested functions, and only in React functions. They exist because React tracks hook order per component instance to pair state between renders. Custom hook example: useFetch(url) that holds data/loading/error state, aborts on unmount and can be reused across components.

questions.text: What is dependency injection in Spring and what problems does it solve?
questions.reference_answer: DI is a pattern where an object's dependencies are supplied from outside (the Spring IoC container) instead of the object constructing them. Benefits: loose coupling against interfaces, easier unit testing with mocks, centralised lifecycle and configuration, and enabling cross-cutting features via proxies (transactions, security). Constructor injection is preferred for immutability and explicit required dependencies.

questions.text: How does @RestController differ from @Controller, and what makes a good REST API design?
questions.reference_answer: @Controller returns view names (MVC); @RestController adds @ResponseBody so every method returns data (JSON) directly. Good REST design: resource-oriented URIs, correct HTTP verbs and status codes, pagination for collections, idempotency semantics, versioning, and consistent error payloads (e.g. RFC 7807 problem+json).

questions.text: Explain the JPA entity lifecycle states and how you would detect and fix the N+1 query problem.
questions.reference_answer: States: new/transient (not managed), managed/persistent (tracked by the persistence context), detached (context closed), removed (scheduled for deletion). N+1: fetching N parent rows triggers N additional lazy queries for children. Detect via SQL logging / Hibernate statistics; fix with JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph / batch fetching, or DTO projections when the children are not needed as entities.

questions.text: Two threads increment the same counter 1000 times each. Why can the result be less than 2000, and how do you fix it?
questions.reference_answer: count++ is read-modify-write, not atomic: both threads can read the same value and lose an update (race condition). Fixes: synchronized block/method, AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet (CAS-based), or a Lock. For higher throughput, shard the counter (LongAdder). Also consider visibility: without happens-before, threads may cache stale values.

questions.text: How do you implement centralised error handling in a Spring Boot REST API?
questions.reference_answer: Use @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods (or @ControllerAdvice + ResponseEntityExceptionHandler) to map exceptions to consistent error payloads with correct status codes. Handle validation errors (MethodArgumentNotValidException) with field-level messages, define custom exceptions for domain rules, and never leak stack traces to clients. Log server-side with correlation IDs.

questions.text: Walk through what happens when a request carrying a JWT hits a Spring Security-protected endpoint.
questions.reference_answer: The filter chain intercepts before the controller: a custom JWT filter (OncePerRequestFilter) reads the Authorization: Bearer header, parses and validates signature/expiry, builds an Authentication with authorities and stores it in the SecurityContext. Authorization rules (authorizeHttpRequests / @PreAuthorize) then decide access; failures yield 401 (unauthenticated) or 403 (unauthorized). Stateless sessions mean no server-side session is created.

questions.text: What is the GIL in Python and what are its practical implications for CPU-bound vs I/O-bound work?
questions.reference_answer: The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time in CPython. CPU-bound multithreading gains nothing (threads take turns); use multiprocessing or native extensions that release the GIL. I/O-bound work benefits from threading or asyncio because the GIL is released during blocking I/O waits.

questions.text: What are decorators in Python and when have you used them? Explain @functools.wraps.
questions.reference_answer: A decorator is a callable that wraps another function to extend behaviour without modifying it — commonly used for caching, auth checks, retries, timing and registration (Flask/FastAPI routes). Without @functools.wraps(wrapper) applied inside a decorator, the wrapper keeps its own __name__/__doc__, breaking introspection and debugging tools.

questions.text: Compare list, tuple and set in Python. When would you use each?
questions.reference_answer: List: ordered, mutable, allows duplicates — for sequences you will change. Tuple: ordered, immutable, hashable — for fixed records and dict keys; safer for constants. Set: unordered, unique members, O(1) membership tests — for de-duplication and set algebra (union/intersection). Immutability makes tuples usable as dict keys and cache-safe.

questions.text: What is a generator and why can it be better than returning a list? Show the idea with yield.
questions.reference_answer: A generator function uses yield to produce values lazily, one at a time, keeping state between calls. Memory stays O(1) regardless of sequence length — ideal for huge files, streams or infinite sequences. Example: def read_large(f): for line in f: yield line.strip() — processes a 10 GB log line-by-line without loading it. Generators are iterators and exhaust after use.

questions.text: When would you pick Django vs FastAPI for a new backend service?
questions.reference_answer: Django: batteries-included — ORM, admin, auth, migrations — ideal for content-heavy, CRUD-driven products where convention and speed of assembly matter. FastAPI: lightweight, async-first, automatic OpenAPI docs and Pydantic validation — ideal for high-throughput microservices and APIs where performance and explicit typing matter. Team familiarity and ecosystem needs usually decide.

questions.text: How do transactions work in SQLAlchemy, and what are common pitfalls?
questions.reference_answer: A Session tracks objects and opens a transaction lazily; commit() flushes pending SQL and commits, rollback() undoes. Sessions should be scoped per request/unit-of-work and closed (context manager). Pitfalls: long-running transactions holding locks, forgetting commit so changes vanish, detached instances accessed after session close (DetachedInstanceError), and the N+1 lazy-load pattern.
